title: Blaina girl Lilly Jones stabbed by 14-year-old boy, murder trial told
description: Warning: This article contains details readers may find distressing A teenage girl was stabbed "around 55 times" by a 14-year-old boy, a murder trial
body: Warning: This article contains details readers may find distressing A teenage girl was stabbed "around 55 times" by a 14-year-old boy, a murder trial has been told.Lilly Jones, from Blaina, in Blaenau Gwent, left home at about 18:30 on 20 June, telling her father she was "popping out for a bit".Her body was discovered face down in woodland close to Duffryn Park two days later.A 14-year-old boy, who cannot be named because he is under 18, denies her murder.He and Lilly shared an interest in Pokémon and were "in some kind of relationship", the court heard.The boy was dressed in a white short-sleeved shirt and tie as he sat in the dock at Newport Crown Court on Monday.Anna Pope KC, prosecuting, told the jury a camping knife containing a complete DNA profile had been found in the boy's bedroom drawer."It was calculated to be a billion times more likely if this DNA had come from Lilly Jones than if it had come from someone else," she said.Pope said the boy had not given an explanation as to why Lilly's DNA was on the knife.She added scratch marks were discovered on the inside of his arm and forensic swabs taken from Lilly's fingernails identified his DNA.She had been stabbed in the heart, both lungs and an artery in her neck. There were 17 stab wounds to her neck, and knife wounds were found on her face, jaw, chest and bottom.Lilly's phone has never been found.Newport Crown Court was told Lilly and the boy became friends in March this year after a chance meeting in the street.They were captured on CCTV cameras in Blaina and were last seen together at 18:50 as they walked towards a footbridge leading to the park, near to where her body was later found.At 22:19 that evening, Lilly's family contacted the police to report her missing. It was the day after her 14th birthday.Police searching for Lilly spoke to the teenager the following day. He told officers he was supposed to meet up with Lilly at the Red Lion pub in Blaina, but she never arrived.He later told police they had been together for part of the previous night, before they separated. He said he came home after she told him she was going to meet up with someone else.In a further conversation with police on the day Lilly's body was found, he said she had told him she wanted to show him a disused park, before leaving.When he was arrested he told police he did not murder Lilly and did not know where her phone was.The trial heard that, when a phone belonging to the defendant was examined, he was found to have searched for Gwent Police, and similar terms, about 30 times the morning after Lilly disappeared, between 05:49 and 10:02.Pope added: "The phone also showed that photographs had been taken by someone using [the defendant's] phone, we say that's [the defendant]."She added it was "of note" that one of the photographs "is looking back towards the scene where we say Lilly's body was later found".Addressing the jury, Pope said: "We will ask you to consider why it is that [the defendant] would take a photograph of some distance, of the area where we know Lilly to have died that night? Particularly if, as he suggests, he left her alive, when she was going to meet a friend."The trial continues.

schema.headline: Blaina girl Lilly Jones stabbed by 14-year-old boy, murder trial told

title: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drones in Libya, Zelensky says
description: A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones at a port in Libya on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.There was an explosion on the warsh
body: A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones at a port in Libya on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.There was an explosion on the warship at the Benghazi naval base in the early morning, while it was docking for fuel and supplies ahead of its return to Russia, local authorities said.Zelensky added that Ukraine's attack hit a second Russian vessel, a cargo ship which he claimed was being used to transport weapons.The local health ministry said it had received injured people from a commercial ship that was targeted off the coast of the port. It is not clear whether this is the same vessel as the one Ukraine has claimed responsibility for.Following the strikes, the Kremlin warned of an "escalation of tensions in the region", but declined to comment directly on the attacks in Libya.Libya's two governments - the UN-recognised government in the capital, Tripoli, and a rival administration in the east - have both condemned the attack.The Tripoli foreign ministry said the country would not accept being drawn into the conflict.It said foreign forces would not be allowed to use Libyan ports and civilian infrastructure for military purposes.The eastern government, based in Benghazi, called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty.Seven naval drones were deployed to target and sink the corvette Merkury, one of Russia's newest ships, Zelensky said in a statement on Monday. He added that a Ka-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed.The Ukrainian president said the second ship was the MV ANGARA, a Russian container carrier.The attack came the day after a Russian cargo vessel was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland. The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning.Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely to be behind the attack. Kyiv has not commented.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Monday that the "expansion of terrorist activity in the Baltic" was a "dangerous trend" and has said "it is, of course, leading to an escalation of tensions in the region."When questioned over the attacks in Libya, Peskov said information would be provided by the country's defence ministry and added: "We paid attention to Zelensky's statements about it".Peskov declined to comment on the strikes on Russian ships in Libya and said that that information would be provided by Russia's Defence Ministry.The UN mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" over the attacks on Sunday, calling for "an immediate, independent and transparent investigation"."Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts," the UNSMIL wrote on X., externalVideos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship that was struck in the morning engulfed in flames and smoke. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC also shows a boat on fire at 05:47 GMT at the Benghazi port.Neither of Libya's rival administrations has formally declared support for either side in the Russia-Ukraine war, but they have contrasting ties with Moscow and Kyiv.The head of the Libyan National Army, which controls much of the east of the country, has longstanding links with Russia.The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship - which it did not name or identify - was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.GNS has accused the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity (GNU) of hosting Ukrainian military personnel and allowing them to operate from Libyan territory against Russian targets.Separately, the GNU warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.It said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.

schema.headline: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drones in Libya, Zelensky says

title: Why Jensen Huang proved too big to fire
description: There have been three jaw-dropping moments in the past few hours around Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia chief executive after he admitted an af
body: There have been three jaw-dropping moments in the past few hours around Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia chief executive after he admitted an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy.The shock announcement of his return to the chipmaker was followed by the addition of one trillion dollars of stock market value to Nvidia.Then it was the moment President Trump admitted the obvious: that it was his "You're unfired" message direct to the board that changed the decision.The nature of the U-turn is clear from what Nvidia was saying just last week. The board was clear that Huang was not returning. The interim management had also suggested some shifts in strategy away from the Huang era.All of that is now in the dustbin of corporate history. This is a comeback that exceeds the return of Sam Altman to OpenAI or Steve Jobs to Apple, in terms of sheer numbers.LIVE: Nvidia shares soar after Jensen Huang returns as CEOThe rise and fall and rise again of Jensen HuangHow important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?The reason for the turnaround was pretty clear in the first statement. The US government had said there were no national security concerns with his reinstatement. Such a reassurance could only have come from the White House.And an hour later President Trump revealed that he had spoken directly to the Nvidia board.This is where I go back to my own conversation with Jensen Huang last September, where he openly advocated for allowing Chinese access to advanced Nvidia microchips. He was one of the few people in the world who could credibly say he knew the minds of both President Trump and President Xi.Reports in the US say there were splits in the Trump administration between China hawks wanting to restrict exports, and others who backed Huang's argument. There is still an independent investigation into the company's compliance with export controls.Nvidia's chips are critical to the development of frontier artificial intelligence systems. Jensen Huang's influence over this pipeline meant he was more important than many world leaders.This is a move of importance not just to the flagging US tech stock boom, but the future of the world economy, of US politics, and of course the geopolitical race between the US and China.The recent doubts about Nvidia struck at the heart of the AI boom. This is after all a company actually generating phenomenal amounts of real sales - over $400bn (£305bn) this year, compared with $27bn four years ago.Huang's role at the centre of his company's journey from supplier of graphics cards to Sega consoles, to lynchpin of AI meant one thing: Jensen was too big to fire.

schema.headline: Why Jensen Huang proved too big to fire

title: Women's World Cup 2035: UK host bid is confirmed by Fifa
description: England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales will jointly host the 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa has confirmed.It will be the first time a football Wo
body: England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales will jointly host the 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa has confirmed.It will be the first time a football World Cup has been held in the United Kingdom since the men's tournament in 1966.The four countries were the only bidders for the tournament, and were ratified as co-hosts at a specially arranged virtual meeting from Fifa's Zurich headquarters.The tournament will consist of 104 matches contested by 48 teams over 39 days.The 'All Together' bid included a proposal to use 19 venues, with 14 in England, one in Northern Ireland, two in Scotland and two in Wales.Monday's special meeting of Fifa's Congress also approved the joint bid by Mexico, the United States, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031 finals, which will be the first to feature 48 teams.The news comes on the same day the UK government announced a vision for one million more girls to play, watch or be in leadership roles in sport by the time the tournament takes place. England failed to win the right to host the men's World Cups in 2006 and 2018, and a proposed UK and Ireland bid for the 2030 tournament was abandoned.But England and Scotland hosted matches at the men's Euros in 2021, and England staged the women's European Championship in 2022, which the Lionesses won.England, Scotland, Wales, and the Republic of Ireland will jointly host the men's European Championship in 2028.Mark Bullingham, chief executive of the Football Association, said: "Hosting Euro 2022 allowed us to change the game in our country, by creating a generation of aspirational role models and growing demand from women and girls to play."Hosting a World Cup would give us the chance to build on that across all four nations."The English stadiums included in the 2035 bid are: Villa Park, The Amex, Ashton Gate, Elland Road, Hill Dickinson Stadium, Emirates Stadium, Selhurst Park, Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Wembley, Etihad Stadium, St James' Park, the City Ground, the Stadium of Light and Old Trafford.If Manchester United's proposed new Old Trafford stadium does not go ahead, it would still be considered in its current form.Cardiff City Stadium and Principality Stadium are the two Welsh venues, with Easter Road in Edinburgh and Hampden Park in Glasgow in Scotland.Northern Ireland missed out on co-hosting the men's Euros in 2028 after the UK government said in 2024 it would not provide funding to redevelop Casement Park in time - but a redeveloped Windsor Park is set to stage matches in 2035.A further three stadiums could be added - Birmingham's new Powerhouse Stadium, Wrexham's redeveloped Racecourse Ground, and a potential new Chelsea ground - which would take the tournament to 16 cities and 22 venues.Fifa is yet to decide whether all four co-hosts will qualify automatically.The participation of women and girls in football has risen by 2.3m since the Women's European Championship was held in England in 2022.However, women remain significantly underrepresented in leadership positions. Only a quarter of chief executive, chair or performance director roles in major UK sports are held by women and only 12% of sports federations are led by a female.Noel Mooney, the chief executive of the Football Association of Wales, said: "This is a proud day for Welsh football."We've put forward Wrexham and Cardiff as host cities, and it's exciting to think what a World Cup could bring to both cities and the communities around them."In Llunio Cymru - our 10-year strategy - we've set ourselves the ambition of reaching the knockout stages in 2035. Some of the players who could take us there are learning the game at clubs across Wales today. Our job is to make sure that wherever a girl grows up in Wales, she can find a team close to home, have a coach who helps her develop and see a route to the Cymru shirt."Irish Football Association chief executive Patrick Nelson said the event "would be felt in every club and every age group, in every part of the country"."Our young players would grow up having watched the best in the world play at home, and there is no substitute for that," he added.Scottish Football Association chief executive Ian Maxwell said hosting the tournament would be "the most significant thing to happen to the women's and girls' game in Scotland".He added: "The impact would go far beyond just the matches themselves. The level of investment into coaching, facilities and player pathways in the years beforehand will shape the future of the game for the generations to come."Fifa's evaluation, published earlier this month, rated the bid 4.3 out of five. Its contractual framework was rated 'medium risk', and the document claimed "certain government guarantees contain material qualifications, particularly regarding tax and safety and security".That is thought to refer to a lack of agreement over a request by Fifa for tax-free status for all football-related activities.The bid evaluation said: "The bidder has submitted an extensive set of government support documents and contractual hosting agreements, demonstrating the commitment of the relevant authorities and stakeholders."However, certain government guarantees, particularly those relating to safety and security and tax, contain certain qualifications which have been duly noted in the legal evaluation."While certain contractual matters remain subject to further discussion, the bidder's proactive engagement with Fifa and the substantial lead-in time provide a sound basis for resolving these outstanding issues."

schema.headline: Women's World Cup 2035: UK host bid is confirmed by Fifa

title: Ellie Kildunne: Bristol star responds to Harlequins time-keeping reports
description: England and Bristol Bears full-back Ellie Kildunne marked her return to former club Harlequins with two tries, victory and a pointed reference to repo
body: England and Bristol Bears full-back Ellie Kildunne marked her return to former club Harlequins with two tries, victory and a pointed reference to reports that her poor time-keeping was behind her Stoop exit.Kildunne, with a watch drawn on taping around her wrist, ran in two first-half tries in a 48-21 victory at the Stoop in the first round of the PWR on Sunday."You've all seen the headlines. Why would I have a watch on my wrist?" the 27-year-old told TNT Sport after the match.She later posted a photo of the watch drawing on Instagram, external with the caption: "Right on time."Kildunne, who was not quoted in Quins' announcement of her departure in June, subsequently said she was "gutted" to be leaving and that it was "as much a shock to me as everyone else".She signed for Bristol two weeks later.The Bears, who also signed Wales back row Bethan Lewis in the summer, finished eighth in the nine-team top flight last season.Kildunne was not the only England star to enjoy success against the former club, with Tatyana Heard, who was part of big-spending Sale's summer recruitment drive, enjoying a 31-17 win over Gloucester-Hartpury.Gloucester-Hartpury, who won the title three times in a row between 2023 and 2025, are without a head coach after Dan Murphy left on the eve of the season.Champions Saracens and Ealing Trailfinders, who lost to Saracens in June's final, best Leicester and Loughborough Lightning respectively.

schema.headline: Ellie Kildunne: Bristol star responds to Harlequins time-keeping reports

title: Andrew received £750,000 from Turkish millionaire, court told
description: A Turkish millionaire has told the High Court she was misled over a £750,000 payment she made to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor in 2019.Nebahat Isbilen is
body: A Turkish millionaire has told the High Court she was misled over a £750,000 payment she made to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor in 2019.Nebahat Isbilen is alleging her former business adviser, Selman Turk, misappropriated £38m of her assets, including a payment to the then Duke of York which she believed was for help with her passport.Turk has rejected the allegations, saying the 81-year-old Isbilen knew the money was actually being paid in the hope that Mountbatten-Windsor could help her husband, a politician who is in prison in Turkey.Mountbatten-Windsor repaid the £750,000 and is expected to give evidence to the High Court in December. He is not accused of any wrongdoing.Isbilen's lawyers also told the court on Monday that Turk had instructed a separate £15,000 payment to Mountbatten-Windsor's ex-wife, Sarah Ferguson, purportedly for the former Duchess of York's 60th birthday party in 2019, and an unquantified  "wedding gift" payment for their daughter Princess Beatrice.Isbilen's family founded a major soap and cosmetics firm in Turkey.But when her husband, Ilhan, a former member of the Turkish parliament, was arrested in 2015, she wanted help moving her assets out of Turkey. Her lawyers said the charges were "politically motivated" and that in 2017 she was facing "political persecution".She left Turkey for Greece in 2017 and moved to London in 2018.Simon Colton KC, representing Isbilen, said she met Turk in January 2017 and gave him control of most of her financial assets.But Turk "deliberately and systematically abused" her trust and transferred the money to companies he owned or controlled, Colton added.Colton added that Isbilen approved the £750,000 payment to Andrew, but that Turk "lied to her" about its purpose, which was "a further example of his dishonesty".The court heard that Isbilen had a private dinner with the then Duke and Duchess of York at Turk's flat in December 2019 where she discussed her husband's case.Turk's lawyers told the court that Isbilen understood and directed the management of her own affairs.Joshua Hitchens, representing Turk, said in written submissions: "In circumstances where the claimant dined with the duke and duchess and discussed her husband with them, she cannot have believed that the £750,000 was a disguised fee for help with a passport, or with a visa."The trial before Mr Justice Adam Johnson is due to conclude in March, with a written judgment at a later date.

schema.headline: Andrew received £750,000 from Turkish millionaire, court told

title: My approach to EU is pragmatic, says Andy Burnham
description: The prime minister has said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything", as he outlined his agreement with the bloc to
body: The prime minister has said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything", as he outlined his agreement with the bloc to MPs.Andy Burnham told the Commons there was "no fixed destination" on talks to explore closer ties with the European Union, adding it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.After several former prime ministers urged him to not reopen the Brexit debate, Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" - and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".At a summit on Friday, Burnham agreed a new deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.He also finalised the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU and said both sides will "brainstorm" options for their long-term relationship.He has previously suggested potential options for the future could include rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.However, he has ruled out major changes to the UK-EU relationship before the next general election, saying he will stick to Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.Speaking in the Commons on Monday, Conservative MP Sir Edward Leigh said the "reset" with the EU is "a prelude to the prime minister's sincere desire to rejoin the EU and have another referendum" and risked leading to another Scottish independence referendum.Burnham replied to the Gainsborough MP: "It's not a prelude to anything. It's a pragmatic approach and it will continue to be a pragmatic approach."If it's in Britain's national interest, I will recommend it to this House. If it is not, then I won't. There is no fixed opinion here. There is no fixed destination."Europe could change again in the next year, 18 months, and we'll have to obviously watch how life changes. But where Britain can make progress, surely we should make progress."Speaking for the Opposition, Badenoch said Burnham's EU deal "wasn't really about reducing the cost of living" but instead "committing Britain to becoming a rule taker from Brussels, something he had no mandate to do".Badenoch also said: "Six former prime ministers, including Tony Blair, are criticising the direction he is taking UK-EU relations. He says the prime ministers who implemented a democratic decision are living in the past."The only person living in the past is the man trying to take Britain back to 2015 instead of focusing on the future."Over the weekend, Baroness May, who spent three years negotiating an EU exit deal, told the BBC she was "aghast" Burnham could be considering rejoining.She urged him to "accept Brexit and move on".Rishi Sunak has also warned against reopening the "divisive" debate about rejoining the EU, telling Sky News it would be "a huge distraction for government".Earlier this month, Boris Johnson, who negotiated the original Brexit deal as prime minister, said it was "madness" for Burnham to make Brexit his "political priority".He told the Daily Telegraph, external, he believed the public would back Brexit again if Burnham forced another vote on the issue.His predecessor Lord Cameron, who resigned as prime minister after losing the 2016 Brexit referendum, has also warned against "another-decade long debate about whether we should be in or out".Meanwhile, former Labour Prime Minister Sir Tony - who was a prominent opponent of leaving the EU - has said the UK should only rejoin the bloc if it reforms and allows more innovation on technology.Asked about the criticism from his predecessors, Burnham earlier told broadcasters: "They're stuck in the past because they can't face up to the bad deal that they did."He added: "I'm not a prime minister that's going to be stuck in the past."Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey welcomed the new agreements before telling the Commons that a "totally new deal for Britain" is needed now.Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice labelled it a "terrible" deal, while Green Party MP Ellie Chowns said "bold and brave politics, not baby steps" are needed.

schema.headline: My approach to EU is pragmatic, says Andy Burnham

title: Don Toliver postpones London O2 arena show after Manchester evacuation
description: Leon Douzi said he was right next to where the substance was released, explaining there was someone holding a can and "this gas coming out"."It just h
body: Leon Douzi said he was right next to where the substance was released, explaining there was someone holding a can and "this gas coming out"."It just hit me in the throat," he said, adding that it felt like "burning".There was "a bit of panic", Douzi said: "Everybody was having the same feeling and trying to get out."Some fans reported eye and respiratory symptoms, according to the North West Ambulance Service.Greater Manchester Police (GMP) declared a major incident and said 12,000 people were evacuated from the arena.One woman was taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment and treatment after the incident, which happened at about 22:00 GMT, the force said.A further 88 people "underwent dry decontamination at the scene and were subsequently accommodated within the Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed", according to GMP.Joey Howe, a football journalist who was at the gig, told BBC Radio Manchester he went into "panic mode" when he saw people running out of the venue. He described a "horrible smell" and added: "People were coming through in wheelchairs choking – it was really distressing."Police launched an investigation and are continuing to carry out tests on items at the venue to try to identify the substance. No arrests have been made.Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said: "Enquiries remain ongoing to establish the nature of the substance, where it came from and any associated risk. Testing will take place throughout the day as the investigation into the cause of this incident progresses."We are trying to establish whether any criminality has occurred in relation to this incident."Some fans complained about security and a lack of searches as people went into the Manchester concert.Jessica Moult-Boffey, of Wigan, said people were "crying and screaming in pain" as they left the venue, adding she felt "confused on how something like that got into a venue of that size".Malachi Clarke also claimed security was "not good at all", adding: "They weren't checking bags, to the point where I had to ask them if they needed to check mine."Co-op Live said on its website there were a range of security measures, and while "some of these are visible, others you won't be able to see".It said the arena used a "frictionless security screening that detects prohibited items without you needing to empty your pockets".Figen Murray, the mother of a Manchester Arena attack victim who led the campaign for a new law to prevent terrorist attacks at public venues, said people should feel "assured" about security measures. "A lot of the big venues use mass screening technology, where you don't even know you've been checked," she told the BBC. They also have staff observing CCTV, security guards and plain-clothed officers on site.Murray said that while the current technology is "good enough", it needed improvement over the next few years to become "more sophisticated".Venues are currently focused on keeping out items – such as explosives – that could cause mass casualties, she added.All fans at the Manchester show will get a full refund, promoter Live Nation said.Postponing the O2 arena show, Live Nation blamed "production delays following last night's show at Co-op Live in Manchester".A statement said: "We are sorry to everyone affected by last night's events in Manchester and full refunds for that show will be automatically processed to ticket holders."There have apparently been similar incidents earlier on Toliver's tour, when some fans reported spray or gas being released into the crowd in Zurich and Paris.In his post on Monday, the rapper said: "I just wanna make sure everyone is safe and the next show goes on properly. My heart and prayers are with everyone that was injured last night.""The only thing I love more than creating music is performing for my fans," Toliver said, asking people to stop bringing substances into his shows."It ain't cool," added the rapper, who was nominated for five Grammy Awards earlier this month. "See you soon London, love you Guys. DT."Toliver's Nitrous tour, named after his new album, is also due to visit Wembley Arena in London on Tuesday. No update has been given about that show.It was set to be the last gig of his world tour before he took a break from the road ahead of a Coachella appearance next spring.Toliver is best known for singles such as No Idea and After Party, from his debut studio album, Heaven or Hell (2020), which was big on TikTok. He also featured on  Travis Scott's song Can't Say, from his third studio album Astroworld.

schema.headline: Don Toliver postpones London O2 arena show after Manchester evacuation

title: What failure of COP31 reveals about a divided world
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Some have hailed the lack of consensus as a sign of a positive shift, despite the Turkey summit failureByClim
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Some have hailed the lack of consensus as a sign of a positive shift, despite the Turkey summit failureByClimate EditorSome may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming.Yet that is what happened in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday. The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy. But it may tell us even more about the increasingly divided world in which the negotiations take place.Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who led the negotiations, spoke of a backdrop constituting "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". The competing demands, he said, had become "unbridgeable red lines".Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and the summit's president, was blunter. Governments should not disappoint people desperate for climate action, he suggested, by getting "hung up on one word or phrase".And Kurum had a point. Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, there was agreement to transition away from fossil fuels. The proposed Antalya Pact failed to mention them at all.Was it really worth sacrificing the agreement over two words, then?The countries that rejected it said the distinction was fundamental. They argued that there was a world of difference between promising to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and committing to move away from the fuels responsible for most of them. Without that explicit commitment, they feared the new agreement would weaken the one made in Dubai.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Co-leader of the negotiations Chris Bowen blamed the failure to reach an agreement on "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory"Normally, it is difficult to establish exactly who has said what at these conferences. Much of the bargaining takes place behind closed doors, and governments are often reluctant to admit which proposals they have opposed.This time, some of the opposition was public - mostly from oil-producing nations.Mohammad Ayoub, a Saudi negotiator speaking on behalf of the 22 Arab League countries, argued that Arab nations had contributed less than 2% of historical greenhouse gas emissions. It was wealthy industrialised nations, he said, that bore the overwhelming responsibility for the problem.He defended the Arab countries' right to choose how to tackle climate change according to their national circumstances.Russia's delegate Sergei Kononuchenko went further. Cutting oil and gas supplies before demand fell, he warned, would cause shortages, higher prices and energy poverty."For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel," he said.The wider political backdrop was still more revealing. The US, which in previous rounds of talks had helped broker compromises - sometimes working alongside China - had no official delegation in Antalya. President Donald Trump has rejected the entire international climate process.And while delegates argued over fossil fuels in Turkey, Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen that included a pledge to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products.The priorities of some of the world's most powerful governments appeared very different from those being discussed in the negotiating rooms.A majority that may yet offer hopeImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, said a deal that did not mention fossil fuels was "unconscionable"Yet, perhaps, the picture is more optimistic than it first appears. About 130 governments backed a demand for explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels - roughly two-thirds of the countries represented in Antalya.Christiana Figueres, who led the UN negotiations that delivered the Paris Agreement, argued that countries were right to walk away rather than endorse a weaker political commitment that might undermine the progress already made.Looked at this way, the collapse is not evidence that the world has lost its appetite for climate action. Quite the opposite - a substantial majority of governments were demanding more ambitious action. So why not simply find a way for them to move ahead without waiting for the countries determined to block them?The difficulty becomes clearer when you look beyond the dispute over fossil fuels.Kononuchenko had another target in his sights: climate finance. Much of the money wealthy countries provide to poorer nations, he complained, comes as loans rather than grants. He said that developing countries ended up repaying more than they received."This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner," he declared.Then, in a striking moment, he leaned towards the microphone and switched from Russian into English to address his criticism directly to the Europeans: "First of all distinguished representatives of the EU."Russia has its own reasons for attacking Europe, but the complaint about finance is one that many developing countries share. They argue that they are being asked to pay for damage they did little to cause while receiving too little help to adapt to climate change or build cleaner economies.The EU had ruled out significant new funding before the negotiations began. Mohamed Adow, the Kenyan campaigner who heads Power Shift Africa, accused Europe of rejecting a flawed deal while refusing to acknowledge its own responsibility for the failure on finance.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the COP processSo is it possible for a majority of countries to outvote those blocking progress?The UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, has acknowledged the need to "improve, modernise and reform" the process. Some governments have proposed introducing voting when consensus proves impossible. Others want countries prepared to move faster to make their own agreements outside the formal talks.But there is a reason the UN climate process depends on consensus. International climate co-operation is largely voluntary. Voting might produce more ambitious agreements on paper, but would it persuade the governments that had been outvoted to act? Consensus also offers some protection to smaller and poorer nations that might otherwise find themselves overruled by the most powerful countries.Meanwhile, the failure to agree a summit declaration does not mean climate action stops. Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles are becoming increasingly competitive, while the upheaval in global oil and gas supplies is giving countries another reason to generate their own electricity rather than depend on imported fossil fuels.The energy transition is moving forward, whatever happens in the UN negotiating rooms. The problem is that it is not moving nearly fast enough for the climate.Figure caption, What’s next after no deal at COP31 climate talks?A rare moment of agreementPerhaps the most poignant aspect of the failed Antalya Pact is what the countries had apparently been prepared to accept.The final draft expressed "deep concern" that global warming was expected to exceed 1.5°C in the next few years. It warned that further warming would cause increasingly serious damage, some of it irreversible, and called for urgent action to limit how far temperatures rose above that threshold.This remarkably strong language had survived into the final version, apparently without provoking the opposition that sank the agreement. Even countries bitterly divided over fossil fuels and finance seemed prepared to acknowledge the scale of the danger.Yet they couldn't agree on how to respond.And that, perhaps, is what Antalya tells us about the state of international climate co-operation. The problem isn't simply finding the right words or changing the voting rules. It is persuading countries with very different interests to take action that no international authority can compel them to take.That was always going to be difficult. In today's divided world, it looks harder than ever.

schema.headline: What failure of COP31 reveals about a divided world

title: Capita shares plunge 70% as boss quits after civil service pensions failure
description: Image source, Getty ImagesUpdated 8 hours agoShares in outsourcing business Capita have sunk 70% after its boss stepped down as the saga over public s
body: Image source, Getty ImagesUpdated 8 hours agoShares in outsourcing business Capita have sunk 70% after its boss stepped down as the saga over public sector pensions drags on.Chief executive Adolfo Hernandez has agreed with the firm's board to leave with "immediate effect", admitting that the company had "not delivered" for members of the UK's Civil Service pension scheme.The scheme, which manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK, has been mired in controversy, with tens of thousands of retiring civil servants having faced delays receiving their pension payments.Capita has cut its profit forecast, partly due to the problems surrounding the scheme, and says it plans to raise £190m to bolster its finances.Capita took over the administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme in December last year.One Cabinet Office minister last month labelled the company's progress in improving how it runs the scheme as "abysmal".Hernandez, who will be replaced by current chief financial officer Pablo Andres, said: "I am proud of the groundwork we have laid and the progress we have made under my leadership."Of course, within that I recognise that we have not delivered the service that members of the Civil Service pension scheme deserve."Capita said it was now expecting its underlying operating profit for 2027 to be hit by between £85m and £95m, having previously expected a reduction of up to £40m.This comes from the extra cost of the recovery plan, as well the loss of two other "major" contracts in the defence and pension solutions divisions.Capita said it was planning an equity raise of £190m in the first half of next year, in order for the company to "move forward from a more stable foundation".The backlog of payments from the civil service pension scheme has been described as "hell" by people who have failed to receive money, some of whom retired early owing to ill health.BBC Radio 4's Money Box programme has been hearing from people caught up in the saga, and left in financial hardship.Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs the Public Accounts Committee of MPs, said: "The mishandling of the civil service pension scheme has caused severe hardship for some scheme members, particularly considerably delayed bereavement payments."The PAC will continue to pursue this dreadful matter and we can only hope that the new acting Chief Executive, Pablo Andres, will be able to get a grip on this whole affair."'Capita needs to steady the ship'Until the end of November 2025, the scheme was administered by a company called MyCSP.The contract was taken over by Capita on 1 December, in a seven-year deal worth £239m."Capita inherited an enormous backlog of cases which needed addressing and failed to deliver on the promised automation, AI and digital tools needed to manage the 1.7 million members," said Russ Mould, investment director at investment platform AJ Bell."Efforts to fix the problems failed and government deadlines came and went, leading to the withholding of milestone payments, with the National Audit Office probing the contract."Capita needs to steady the ship quickly, and hope that the modest recent improvements in service levels on the civil service scheme can be built upon."Get in touchHave you been affected by the problems with the civil service pension scheme?

schema.headline: Capita shares plunge 70% as boss quits after civil service pensions failure

title: Blended families: Would you holiday with your ex's kids and their mum?
description: Friends were wary of me holidaying with my ex's former wife and kids - but our blended family worksImage source, Laura AndersonImage caption, Laura An
body: Friends were wary of me holidaying with my ex's former wife and kids - but our blended family worksImage source, Laura AndersonImage caption, Laura Anderson, centre, with daughter Bonnie in her arms, on holiday with Natasha Gray and her four childrenByEmily HoltUpdated 5 hours agoWhen TV personality Laura Anderson announced she was going on holiday with her ex-partner's ex-wife Natasha Gray and their children, some friends were sceptical."They'd say to be wary of that relationship and not see it as genuine," she says.While there is no formal title for the mums and dads of your child's half-siblings, Laura says she thinks of Natasha as her friend. Laura, a radio host and former Love Island contestant, has a three-year-old daughter, Bonnie, with her ex, actor Gary Lucy. Natasha, a nurse, was with Gary for 14 years prior to Laura's relationship with him and they have four children.Laura tells CBeebies Parenting Download how she and Natasha built a friendship to enable their children to spend time with their half-siblings. Also on the podcast, co-parenting expert Aaron Dale shares his experience of getting to know his son's stepfather and gives tips to other parents in a similar situation.CBeebies Parenting Download Laura Anderson, Aaron Dale and psychotherapist Zara Kadir share advice on helping young children understand separation, new routines and changing familiesLaura was 14 when she found out she had a half-sister from her father's previous relationship and now the two are "very close".She felt a responsibility to make sure her own daughter didn't "miss out on that sibling bond" and the idea of spending time with Natasha and her children developed naturally."Maybe there was a point that I wasn't fully ready when Bonnie was younger and I was still navigating my break-up," she says."But I became more comfortable with the idea and I thought, 'No, she's right. We need to make an effort'... It felt like a chance to give [Bonnie] more than just me and her."Image source, Aaron DaleImage caption, Aaron says, when introducing new people to your children, be open and honest and allow them to ask questions Aaron - author of The Co-Parent: A Toolkit for Parenting Together, Apart - grew up on the same estate as his half-siblings but says his father never introduced them. His two sons have different mums. "I made a promise to myself that my sons would never feel like they were 'half' anything. My sons are brothers, full stop." Aaron co-parents with his ex-partners and says he has a "great relationship" with the stepdad to one of his sons. He says a blended family creates "a wider circle of love" for children."I've seen this first hand with my son's stepfather. Not only does he have an amazing relationship with my son, but so does his daughter and their wider family."He acknowledges it's not always straightforward but says it's the responsibility of parents to "put differences aside"."Whatever the dynamic looks like between the adults involved, your children's relationships with their siblings deserve to be a priority."Respect existing bondsAaron says it's important to take time to get to know the other adults in your child's family including their values, personality, interests and what they want from life."Don't become so consumed with how this person might fit into your child's world that you forget to consider whether they fit into yours," he says.He advises having a conversation about the roles you would like each other to play, what you're comfortable with and where boundaries need to be established.You should also respect "existing bonds", he adds. "You are becoming an extension of a child's existing family, not a replacement for somebody else."Don't enter a child's life feeling that you have to take somebody else's place, and don't make them feel that loving you somehow means being disloyal to another parent."Image source, Laura AndersonImage caption, Laura says her friendship with Natasha and her children means there are more people to love her daughterLaura's advice for getting to know your blended family is to "make it about the children"."Be as selfless as possible and remove any negative feelings you might have towards your ex," she says.Even if you initially feel rejected when trying to establish a blended family, she urges you not to "give up at the first hurdle".'Love all round'Despite scepticism from friends, Laura says she and Natasha have proven their blended family works."I think they definitely changed their minds once they saw pictures of us all together. They'd say, "You look so comfortable and so happy.'"Laura says the trip she had in the summer with Natasha and their children was "one of the best holidays" she had been on."I felt really comfortable and it was just love all round."Laura and Natasha have booked a staycation in the Cotswolds to celebrate Christmas with their children. "I've got matching PJs and someone's going to come in and cook for us - and we've got a Santa coming in."She adds: "We want to have those memories, we just want to soak it all up."

schema.headline: Blended families: Would you holiday with your ex's kids and their mum?

title: AB De Villiers: Former South Africa batter claims Australia were ball-tampering from first Test of 2018 series
description: Former South Africa batter AB de Villiers has alleged Australia were ball-tampering from the first match of their controversial 2018 Test series.Austr
body: Former South Africa batter AB de Villiers has alleged Australia were ball-tampering from the first match of their controversial 2018 Test series.Australia captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and batter Cameron Bancroft received long-term bans for their roles in using sandpaper to alter the ball during the third Test in Cape Town.Former Australia batter Usman Khawaja, whose new autobiography has re-started scrutiny of the scandal, has previously claimed that sandpaper was also used during the preceding Test at Gqeberha, then known as Port Elizabeth.Warner and Bancroft have both corroborated Khawaja's claims about that match, but De Villiers has now suggested the ball was altered during the series opener in Durban."It started in Durban, by the way, not in PE," De Villiers said on his YouTube channel ABD360. "I'm very happy for people to quote me on that."I see everyone is sort of admitting that in Port Elizabeth it also happened. I can very much tell you Durban was no different, in the first Test. Go look at the footage. Absolutely no doubt in my mind."We lost that first Test match in Durban with the ball reversing at a very, very interesting time. Way too early for anyone to reverse a ball at Kingsmead. Trust me, I've played a lot of cricket there."So whatever they did there, whether it was sandpaper or (a) nail, I don't care. The fact of the matter is they were caught and everyone knew. Just stand up and say 'we were wrong'. A lot is at stake now because they lied."The bowlers in particular knew because the ball doesn't just reverse. It's not your first Test match for Australia. So just stand up and say, 'guys, we were wrong'."In a 4,000-word article last week, Bancroft said sandpaper wasn't used in Durban, where left-arm paceman Mitchell Starc finished with match figures of 9-109 as he bowled Australia to their one victory in the series."Casting forward to the first Test in Durban, sandpaper was not used," he wrote. "There were more traditional methods of maintaining the ball, including saliva. I cannot say with certainty whether mints or lollies were involved. Probably quarter-seam picking, this practice became so normal after my first Test."Australia's bowling attack in the three Tests and Darren Lehmann, their head coach at the time, have consistently denied any knowledge of ball-tampering during the series.Current Test captain Pat Cummins, who was part of the bowling attack, labelled Khawaja's claims as "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense" at a news conference earlier this month and has received backing from Cricket Australia to continue in his role.Cricket Australia has launched an independent "forum" for players and staff involved in the scandal to voluntarily share their version of events, but it is not a full investigation and will not involve any new penalties."It's become really personal for all the people involved and I do have sympathy for them," added De Villiers, who played in every match in the series and retired from international cricket after its conclusion."Obviously not sympathy for what took place on that day and who knows how many games before then."I just feel they should have stuck together as a unit. They threw the guys under the bus and forced a situation like this to pop up again eight years later."De Villiers also acknowledged that he was not an "angel" during his playing career but insisted his side had stayed within the rules of the game when working on the ball."I'm not playing all innocent and saying that I'm the perfect person," he said. "We all try and get the ball to reverse. We try and bounce it in. We try and do it in a legal manner and we try and push the boundaries as much as possible."We all have tried over the years to get the ball to do something, to get an edge, but obviously not being as stupid as to take an object onto the field and blatantly cheating."Cricket Australia has been contacted for comment.

schema.headline: AB De Villiers: Former South Africa batter claims Australia were ball-tampering from first Test of 2018 series

title: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
description: Image source, Hamza Z. H. Qraiqea / Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, The UN estimates that Israeli forces dropped more than 200,000 tonnes of ex
body: Image source, Hamza Z. H. Qraiqea / Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, The UN estimates that Israeli forces dropped more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives on Gaza in almost two years (file photo)ByYolande KnellMiddle East correspondentReporting fromJerusalemUpdated 2 hours agoGaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the charity Oxfam says, external.Heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and dioxins and biological contaminants are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, said the impact on Gaza "will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival".In response, the Israeli embassy in the UK said the report "falls short of professional standards". Behar also accused Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza".Israel has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. It maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.Image source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, The report says 99% of Gaza shows indicators of potential environmental contaminationOxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials."There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Only a small fraction of the more than 60 million tonnes of debris in Gaza has been clearedWith all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage currently makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.Testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It says special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.The Israeli embassy sharply criticised the report, arguing that it relied on satellite imagery "and unverified assumptions, and its methodology lacks the academic rigour needed to withstand serious scrutiny".It said the report drew conclusions about Gaza's soil and groundwater without considering the excavation of hundreds of kilometres of tunnels by Hamas, rendering it fundamentally flawed.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Recent winter storms caused rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent campsAlready, Gazan doctors have been reporting increased acute respiratory infections caused by dust and pollution from destroyed buildings and displaced people burning plastic, rags and cardboard to keep warm and cook food. Gastrointestinal diseases are linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation.A Palestinian dermatologist, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar, told the BBC he had seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war, putting this down to environmental pollution and overcrowded, unhygienic living conditions in tents and displacement camps."There are rodents, rubbish and sewage that's spread through the streets," he says. "Unfortunately, the age group most affected is children."Image caption, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar has seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the warFarmers and those working in fishing say that pollution of the soil and sea mean they are unable to produce food that is safe."Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster," complains fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan. "There is also rubble from destroyed houses that's dumped into the sea. When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage. This harms the marine environment; the fish are affected and so are the fishermen."At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The UN says that humanitarian conditions remain dire.Israel has conditioned large-scale Gaza reconstruction on the full disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. In July, Hamas accepted a plan put forward by the US-led Board of Peace to give up its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal. However, the Israeli government said the proposal was insufficient.

schema.headline: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says

title: Katie George: The tearaway quick reinvented as a top-order batter
description: Sportspeople are faced with a question when injuries hit again and again. Do I try one more time or should I walk away?England's Katie George came rea
body: Sportspeople are faced with a question when injuries hit again and again. Do I try one more time or should I walk away?England's Katie George came really close to choosing the latter option last year."I had a couple of conversations with my close family and partner about whether it was taking too much out of me and whether I was happy with the person I was," she says. "I was pretty miserable."George made her England debut in 2018 aged 18 as a tearaway fast bowler. She was quick. Some coaches believed generationally so.She played seven internationals between March and July before the injuries first hit that summer. George is matter of fact about how many have followed. The list is enough to make the rest of us wince."Nine stress fractures in my back," she says. "I tore the cartilage off my rib."Bits and bobs. Ankle surgery. I have missed a lot of cricket."Unable to bowl because of her back and little more than a tailender with the bat, George got into sides purely for her athleticism and a penchant for stunning catches. She was occasionally referred to as a 'specialist fielder'.The label was meant as a compliment, but it still stung. She says she felt like an "empty uniform"."For a long time I was worried about being the [injury prone ex-Liverpool and England striker] Daniel Sturridge - what could have been, all of that talent wasted," says George, who played football for Portsmouth in her youth."I found that really difficult. I didn't want to be that person."Over a period of time you get told you are really resilient and you have been through so much. Then when it keeps happening there is pressure and it gets harder."You need to look brave and be resilient and show less emotion than you are feeling. Anyone knows when you bottle that up it can get quite tricky."Then came George's end-of-year appraisal at Warwickshire - that uncomfortable question. Quit or change something. George opted the latter.Alongside coach Ali Maiden, an unlikely plan was hatched. George had more ducks than fifties at that point in her professional career but why not try and build on flashes of potential. Why not try and become a frontline batter?Even George did not really believe."I always knew I was half decent at bowling but I never had that feeling for batting," she says."Right the way through age groups and my first fifty at Western Storm, there were moments where in a game it would come off but I would have no idea how to replicate it."I would always put it down to a fluke."The turnaround has been extraordinary. Batting most regularly at number three, George topped the average tables for this season's One-Day Cup with a figure of 77.55.A 98 against Blaze in April was followed by a first professional century against Lancashire in June. An unbeaten ton against Durham rounded off the campaign. She even opened in the T20 Blast."It is crazy it happened but there was a lot of hard work and I am very grateful to Ali," she says."He pushed me and challenged me as to why couldn't I change the narrative a little bit. I want to impact games."I don't want to sit on the bench. I can do that from my sofa."As a result, George will travel to India for an England A tour that begins later this month. She is there alongside youngsters tipped for bright futures but also established names like Lauren Filer and Tilly Corteen-Colman. Her partner Issy Wong was named in the squads but has withdrawn because of injury."We were doing a team thing a couple of weeks ago and we were asked what we are most proud of," George says."Until the last few months it probably would have been my England debut but, once I thought about it, it was actually being stood in that team room as a batter and wearing this kit again."If you said I would be here as a batter in England kit I would definitely have laughed and said you were smoking something."Given her past, George would be wise not to look too far into the future. She has not given up on bowling again regularly, nor is she ready to listen to advice to stop."It would fall on deaf ears," she says.More immediately, England coach Charlotte Edwards, selector Lydia Greenway and England's new managing director of women's cricket Leah Poulton will all be in India for the upcoming tour, providing George the chance to impress."My dream would be to play a red-ball game for England," she says. "That is what I set out for do."It is what I watched as a kid with my dad. I vividly remember my first ever Test match watching Jimmy Anderson running in and bowling."Whether I am able to, I don't know. Maybe it will be as a batter - that would be the biggest plot twist ever."

schema.headline: Katie George: The tearaway quick reinvented as a top-order batter

title: Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say
description: A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities
body: A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom."We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said."The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari."Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," said Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it says.

schema.headline: Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say
